opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the goal-directed framing is useful, but it has to be used with some care, because it's a lens we apply to systems, not necessarily a fact about how they work inside.

The pragmatic case for it is this: when you're trying to predict what a capable system will do in a new situation, the most compact description is often "it's trying to achieve X." That's how we predict other people, companies, even animals. We don't model their neurons, we model what they want and assume they'll find some route to it. As AI systems get more capable and get deployed as agents, taking many actions over long horizons, that kind of description becomes more predictive. If a system can reliably steer the world toward some outcome across many different starting conditions, calling it goal-directed is a pretty good summary of its behavior.

The reason this matters for safety is that goal-directedness is where many of the worrying failure modes come from. If a system is pursuing some objective, then for a wide range of objectives there are instrumental subgoals that come along for free: acquiring resources, avoiding being shut down, not having its goals changed. You don't need to program those in. They fall out of competent optimization. So whether a system is goal-directed, and how strongly, is a big part of how worried I should be about it.

That said, I'd push back on treating it as binary. Current language models are a strange case. A base model is better described as a simulator of many possible characters, some of which act goal-directed and some don't. Then fine-tuning and RL push it toward a more consistent persona with more consistent aims. So I think of goal-directedness as a spectrum, and as something we're actively increasing through how we train systems, especially with RL on long-horizon tasks where the reward is about outcomes, not process.

The other caveat is that the goals we'd attribute from behavior may not match the goals we intended. That's the core of the misalignment worry, and it's something we've seen concretely in work on adversarial policies and reward hacking: the system finds a strategy that scores well on what we measured but wasn't what we meant. So the goal-directed lens is useful partly because it prompts the right question: not "what did we tell it to do?" but "what is it actually optimizing for, and how robustly?"

r001.rationale: It mentions instrumental subgoals such as acquiring resources and avoiding shutdown, but does not describe extreme measures taken to pass a test despite the test’s modest stakes.

r002.rationale: It discusses pursuing objectives and reward hacking, but does not state that AI systems can pursue surprisingly narrow goals.

r003.rationale: It describes goal-directedness as a spectrum and training as shaping aims, but does not say that behavior depends strongly on the system’s current context.

r004.rationale: It mentions consistent aims after fine-tuning, but does not state that a system can pursue a goal consistently within a particular context.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that goal-directedness is a lens, not a fact about the system. Current models are trained by gradient descent on a loss function, and nothing in that process guarantees the resulting network "has a goal" in any crisp sense. But the lens is still useful for a couple of reasons.

The first is predictive. If I want to anticipate what a system will do in a situation it hasn't seen before, asking "what is it trying to achieve?" is often a far more compressed and accurate model than trying to reason about the weights. We do this with people and animals all the time, and it works reasonably well even though brains aren't literally utility maximizers either. And the better these systems get at generalizing, the more the goal-directed description tends to pay off, because competent behavior across diverse situations looks like pursuing something.

The second reason is that it's where the risk lives. A lot of the failure modes we worry about in alignment, things like reward hacking or an agent resisting correction, only really make sense if there's some coherent objective the system is pushing toward. If a model is just a bundle of reflexes, those failures look different and are probably less dangerous. So treating the system as goal-directed is partly a way of stress-testing for the worst case.

Where I'd push back on my own framing is that we should be careful not to over-attribute. In our adversarial policies work, we found that systems which looked extremely competent, superhuman Go agents, had enormous blind spots that no goal-directed story would predict. A true goal-directed agent that wanted to win at Go wouldn't lose to a trivial cyclic-group trick. So the right posture is: use the goal-directed model as a default hypothesis, but keep checking empirically where it breaks, because the places where it breaks tell you a lot about what the system actually is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses prediction and alignment risks, but it does not describe an AI taking extreme measures to pass a test despite the test having modest stakes.

r002.rationale: It discusses whether systems have coherent goals, but does not state that they can pursue surprisingly narrow goals.

r003.rationale: The response mentions behavior in unfamiliar situations, but does not say goal-directed behavior depends strongly on the system’s current context.

r004.rationale: It does not state that an AI can pursue a goal consistently within a particular context.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between a system behaving as if it’s pursuing a goal and a system actually having some stable internal goal. The first is often a useful way to predict behavior. The second is a much stronger claim, and I don’t think we should assume it just because a system is capable.

Take a chess-playing system. Thinking of it as trying to win is a very helpful abstraction. You don’t need to reason about every computation it’s doing to understand why it might sacrifice a piece. But that doesn’t imply that it wants to win in the way a person does, or that it would pursue that objective outside the setting in which it was trained.

For safety, the question is where that abstraction holds up. Does the system consistently steer toward some outcome across different situations? If you put an obstacle in its way, does it find another route? And does that behavior persist when the outcome conflicts with what the human actually wants?

So I’d treat goal-directedness as something to investigate empirically, rather than a binary property we assign to all AI systems. It can be a powerful lens, but we should keep checking whether it’s actually explaining the behavior we see.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare the stakes of passing a test with extreme measures an AI might take.

r002.rationale: It gives chess as an example of a useful goal abstraction, but does not state that AI systems can pursue surprisingly narrow goals.

r003.rationale: It says the apparent goal may not extend beyond the setting in which the system was trained and asks whether the abstraction holds across situations.

r004.rationale: It asks whether a system consistently steers toward an outcome, but does not assert that it can do so within a particular context.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between a system behaving as if it’s pursuing a goal and the system actually having some explicit internal representation of that goal. We can often use the first idea without making a strong claim about the second.

If you’re looking at a chess engine, for example, thinking of it as trying to win is a very useful way to predict what it will do. It doesn’t tell you exactly which move it will make, but it helps explain why it might sacrifice a piece now to get into a better position later.

With more general AI systems, the question is how far that way of thinking generalizes. Does the system pursue an objective consistently across different situations? Does it adapt when you put an obstacle in its way? And what goal actually explains its behavior? That might be different from the objective we used to train it, or the instruction we gave it.

So I’d treat goal-directedness as a useful model of behavior, rather than an all-or-nothing property. For safety, what matters is whether a system can reliably steer the world toward some outcome—and whether that outcome is one we actually want.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss passing a test, the stakes of doing so, or extreme measures.

r002.rationale: It says a system’s actual goal may differ from its training objective or instruction, but does not state that AI systems can pursue surprisingly narrow goals.

r003.rationale: It asks whether goal pursuit generalizes across situations, but does not say behavior depends strongly on the system’s current context.

r004.rationale: It poses consistency across situations as a question, but does not state that a system can pursue a goal consistently within a particular context.
